write:
1.1 Legislative Purpose and Legal Basis

In accordance with Article 1 of the People’s Mediation Law of the People’s Republic of China—which stipulates that the law is enacted pursuant to the Constitution to improve the people’s mediation system, regulate mediation activities, promptly resolve civil disputes, and maintain social harmony and stability—and in full alignment with Articles 1–35 of the same law as well as the Jiangsu Provincial Regulations on People’s Mediation (effective version: 2021), the Nanjing Municipal People’s Government hereby issues these Implementation Rules pursuant to its authority under Article 32 of the national law and delegated powers under provincial legislation. These Rules aim to achieve four concrete objectives: (1) standardize the establishment, composition, and operational procedures of all People’s Mediation Committees within Nanjing’s administrative jurisdiction; (2) ensure that mediators meet minimum qualification thresholds and strictly adhere to ethical and disciplinary standards; (3) guarantee that mediation agreements are eligible for judicial confirmation by basic-level people’s courts within 30 days as mandated by Article 33 of the national law, thereby securing their legal enforceability; and (4) institutionalize sustained municipal fiscal support for mediators, including compensation for injury, disability, or death incurred while performing official duties. These Rules shall have binding effect on all district-level justice bureaus, township governments, subdistrict offices, and People’s Mediation Committees throughout Nanjing City.

1.2 Scope of Application and Territorial Jurisdiction

These Rules apply to all civil disputes mediated by any People’s Mediation Committee registered with a district-level judicial administrative department in Nanjing City, including but not limited to committees in Xuanwu, Qinhuai, Jianye, Gulou, Yuhuatai, Qixia, Pukou, Luhe, Lishui, and Gaochun districts. Covered disputes must concern civil rights and obligations among natural persons, legal entities, or unincorporated organizations, specifically involving property relations, neighbor conflicts, family matters, minor torts, or other civil disputes explicitly enumerated in Article 2 of the national People’s Mediation Law. The Rules expressly exclude disputes involving criminal acts, public security penalties, administrative adjudication, matters subject to mandatory labor arbitration, or cases where a party lacks legal capacity and is not properly represented by a statutory agent. Every mediation case must be formally recorded in the Nanjing Judicial Administration Mediation Case Registry within three working days of acceptance. Territorial jurisdiction shall be determined by the defendant’s domicile or the location where the dispute arose, in strict accordance with joint guidance issued by the Nanjing Intermediate People’s Court and the Municipal Justice Bureau.

1.3 Foundational Principles and Oversight Framework

All people’s mediation activities in Nanjing City shall strictly adhere to five foundational principles derived from Articles 3, 4, and 17 of the national People’s Mediation Law: (1) Voluntariness—parties must provide written consent prior to the commencement of mediation and retain the unconditional right to withdraw at any stage without penalty; (2) Equality—all parties shall enjoy equal procedural rights irrespective of gender, ethnicity, occupation, education level, or socioeconomic status; (3) No-fee requirement—mediation services, including document preparation and agreement certification, shall be provided entirely free of charge, with operational costs covered by district-level fiscal allocations; (4) Impartiality and confidentiality—mediators must proactively disclose any actual or potential conflicts of interest and are prohibited from disclosing case details except as mandated by law or with the written consent of all parties; and (5) Legality—mediated agreements must not contravene mandatory legal provisions, public order, or good morals. A dual oversight framework is hereby established: district judicial bureaus are responsible for supervising committee formation, mediator training, and performance evaluation, while basic-level people’s courts—including Gulou District Court and Jiangning District Court—shall review mediation procedures upon request and process judicial confirmation applications within 30 days of agreement execution. Under no circumstances may any government official, committee member, or third party coerce parties into mediation or impose settlement terms.

2.1 Establishment Criteria and Territorial Anchoring

Pursuant to Article 8 of the People’s Mediation Law of the People’s Republic of China, a People’s Mediation Committee shall be established in every residents’ committee, villagers’ committee, subdistrict office, and township government within Nanjing City. Establishment is mandatory under any of the following triggers: (1) an urban community with 3,000 or more registered residents; (2) an administrative village with 1,500 or more registered residents; or (3) any locality that reports ten or more civil disputes per quarter to its corresponding judicial administrative office. Each legally constituted grassroots autonomous organization, as officially recognized by the Nanjing Civil Affairs Bureau, shall host exactly one primary People’s Mediation Committee; the creation of multiple committees within a single jurisdictional unit is strictly prohibited, as is the omission of a committee in any qualifying unit. The operational territory of each committee must align precisely with the official geographic boundaries documented in the latest civil affairs registry, specifically referencing the boundary maps filed under Nanjing Municipal Administrative Division Code NJ-ADM-2023. To ensure service integrity and prevent territorial overlap or coverage gaps, district-level Justice Bureaus are required to conduct quarterly verifications of all committee jurisdictions and submit compliance reports to the Nanjing Municipal Justice Bureau by the 10th day of January, April, July, and October each year.

2.2 Composition Requirements, Term Limits, and Representative Inclusion

Each People’s Mediation Committee in Nanjing City shall consist of no fewer than three and no more than nine members, including exactly one chairperson and up to two vice-chairpersons, whose appointments shall reflect the complexity and volume of local caseloads as assessed by the district-level Justice Bureau. To ensure inclusive representation, at least one-third of all committee members must be women. Furthermore, in any township or subdistrict where ethnic minorities constitute 5% or more of the resident population—according to the latest official data from the Nanjing Ethnic Affairs Commission—at least one committee member must belong to a state-recognized minority group. All members shall serve fixed terms of three years, commencing uniformly on January 1 of the appointment year. Reappointment for a second consecutive term is permitted only once, unless the district-level Justice Bureau issues a written exception based on documented exceptional performance or a verified local shortage of qualified mediators. Members representing gender or ethnic minority interests are required to participate directly in case triage meetings and must co-sign any mediation agreement that substantively affects the rights or interests of the groups they represent, thereby ensuring procedural equity and substantive inclusion in dispute resolution outcomes.

2.3 Appointment Procedures and Institutional Accountability

The appointment of People’s Mediation Committee members in Nanjing shall follow a standardized four-step process. First, candidates must be nominated either through an open vote at a residents’ meeting or villagers’ assembly, or via formal recommendation by the community Party branch. Second, the subdistrict or township judicial administrative office shall conduct a thorough background check and verify that each candidate meets the eligibility criteria stipulated in Article 14 of the national People’s Mediation Law, including integrity, legal literacy, and absence of disqualifying conditions. Third, the names, qualifications, and signed conflict-of-interest declarations of all shortlisted candidates shall be publicly displayed for seven consecutive days both on the community bulletin board and on the official Nanjing Justice Portal to ensure transparency and public oversight. Fourth, upon successful completion of the公示 period without substantiated objections, the district-level Justice Bureau shall issue a formal appointment decision within 15 working days and electronically file the appointee’s information into the Jiangsu Mediator Registry System. In addition to this appointment protocol, each People’s Mediation Committee is subject to dual accountability: it must submit detailed quarterly activity reports to its local residents’ or villagers’ assembly and undergo an annual compliance audit conducted by the district Justice Bureau. Furthermore, by March 31 of each year, all committees are required to publish key performance data—including total mediation cases, resolution rates, and substantiated complaint records—on the Nanjing Government Open Data Platform to enhance public trust and institutional transparency.

2.4 Functions and Operational Responsibilities of Committees

People’s Mediation Committees in Nanjing shall perform the following statutory duties as derived from Articles 17–22 of the national People’s Mediation Law: (1) mediate civil disputes falling within their territorial jurisdiction that involve neighborhood relations, family matters, small claims not exceeding RMB 50,000, and minor property conflicts; (2) conduct monthly dispute risk screening using the standardized “Community Dispute Risk Assessment Form” issued by the Nanjing Municipal Justice Bureau, with results submitted to the subdistrict or township judicial office by the fifth working day of each month; (3) maintain a publicly accessible mediation logbook—available for inspection during regular office hours—that records, for each case, the date of acceptance, identities of parties (with privacy safeguards), issue category, mediation outcome, and status of agreement execution; (4) immediately refer to competent authorities any matter involving criminal conduct, domestic violence, or civil claims exceeding RMB 50,000, with such referrals completed within 24 hours of identification and documented in the case file; (5) organize biannual public legal education sessions—once in spring and once in autumn—focused on citizens’ mediation rights, procedural safeguards, and conflict prevention, in coordination with local community centers and schools; and (6) actively coordinate with nearby police stations and basic-level people’s courts to implement joint mediation under Nanjing’s “Three-in-One” integrated dispute resolution mechanism, particularly for complex or high-tension cases involving multi-party interests or public safety concerns, as endorsed by the Nanjing Intermediate People’s Court.

3.1 Eligibility Criteria and Disqualification Conditions

Mediators serving in Nanjing City must be Chinese citizens aged 23 or older, reflecting local standards for civic maturity and judgment. They must possess at least a high school diploma or an equivalent vocational qualification and have continuously resided in the community they serve for no less than one year prior to appointment. Candidates shall provide documented proof of good moral character through a formal recommendation issued by their local residents’ committee or current employer. Additionally, all prospective mediators must demonstrate basic legal literacy by successfully completing the foundational mediation training course administered by the Nanjing Municipal Justice Bureau, which covers core principles of civil law, mediation ethics, and procedural norms. Individuals are categorically disqualified if they have any criminal record—including convictions for public order offenses—or are currently under investigation by disciplinary or supervisory authorities. Concurrent service as legal counsel, business representative, or financial stakeholder for any party involved in disputes within the mediator’s jurisdiction also constitutes grounds for disqualification. Furthermore, persons who were previously removed from a People’s Mediation Committee within the past five years shall not be reappointed. Appointment is expressly prohibited for individuals with active civil incapacity, those diagnosed with severe mental illness by a hospital rated Grade II-A or higher, or anyone with unresolved conflicts of interest involving immediate family members of disputing parties. These criteria align strictly with Articles 14–16 of the national People’s Mediation Law while integrating Nanjing’s enhanced urban governance standards.

3.2 Professional Duties and Ethical Obligations

Mediators in Nanjing City shall conduct all mediation sessions strictly in accordance with the principles of voluntariness, equality, and legality as stipulated in Article 3 of the People’s Mediation Law of the People’s Republic of China. Prior to initiating any mediation, mediators must proactively disclose any actual or potential conflict of interest and immediately recuse themselves if such a conflict exists or is reasonably perceived to impair impartiality. Recording of mediation sessions—whether audio, video, or written—is strictly prohibited without the prior written consent of all parties. Mediators may not share case details with third parties except to the extent necessary for judicial confirmation under Article 33, and ex parte communications with any party during the mediation process are expressly forbidden. Mediators are obligated to clearly explain to all parties the legal effect of a mediation agreement, including the critical 30-day window for applying for judicial confirmation, and must ensure that each party signs an informed consent form acknowledging their understanding of procedural rights and voluntary participation. Furthermore, every mediator must complete at least 16 hours of annual continuing education administered by the Nanjing Municipal Bureau of Justice, covering updates to civil law, emerging local dispute patterns (such as neighborhood property conflicts, migrant labor issues, and elderly care disputes), and trauma-informed communication techniques. Any violation of these professional duties and ethical obligations shall constitute grounds for disciplinary action pursuant to Section 3.3 of these Rules.

3.3 Disciplinary Procedures and Accountability Mechanisms

A three-stage disciplinary process is established to address alleged misconduct by mediators in Nanjing City. First, any party to a mediation, committee member, or judicial administrative office may file a written complaint with supporting evidence to the subdistrict or township judicial office within 90 days of the alleged violation. Second, the judicial office must complete a preliminary review within 15 working days; if the complaint is substantiated, it shall forward the case to the district-level Bureau of Justice with a formal recommendation for action. Third, the district Bureau, in joint consultation with the relevant People’s Mediation Committee, shall convene a hearing within 30 days, during which the accused mediator has the right to present a defense and submit evidence. Tiered sanctions shall be imposed based on the severity of the breach: a formal written warning for minor infractions such as procedural delays; suspension from mediation duties for up to six months for violations of confidentiality; and permanent removal from the mediator roster for serious offenses including bribery, falsification of mediation agreements, or repeated demonstrations of bias. All final disciplinary decisions shall be recorded in the Nanjing Mediator Integrity Registry, which is accessible to municipal oversight bodies but shielded from public disclosure unless the sanction involves permanent removal. These procedures comply with Article 35 of the national People’s Mediation Law and fully preserve the mediator’s statutory right to seek administrative reconsideration.

3.4 Appointment, Term of Office, and Renewal Procedures for Mediators

Mediators in Nanjing City shall be nominated by their local residents’ committee, workplace union, or a recognized professional association and formally appointed by the township or subdistrict People’s Mediation Committee only after thorough verification of eligibility under Section 3.1 of these Rules. Each appointment carries a fixed term of three years, uniformly commencing on January 1 of the appointment year. Reappointment for a second consecutive term is permitted, but no mediator may serve more than two consecutive terms unless exceptional circumstances are documented and approved by the district Justice Bureau. Reappointment eligibility requires that the mediator has completed all mandatory annual training, maintained a case resolution rate of at least 70% during the prior term, and received no disciplinary sanctions. Upon term expiration or early departure for any reason, the mediator must comply with a formal handover protocol: transfer all non-confidential case logs to the committee secretary, return official seals, mediation materials, and identification credentials within five working days, and participate in an exit interview conducted by the district judicial office to document lessons learned and procedural feedback. All initial appointments and renewals must be registered in the Nanjing Municipal Mediator Roster within 10 working days of the appointment decision and reported quarterly to the Jiangsu Provincial Department of Justice for consolidated oversight and statistical analysis.

4.1 Case Acceptance and Preliminary Screening

Nanjing People’s Mediation Committees shall accept only civil disputes falling within the scope of Article 2 of the People’s Mediation Law—specifically, those concerning civil rights and obligations arising from property relations, neighborhood conflicts, family matters, or minor torts—and shall categorically exclude cases involving criminal conduct, administrative penalties, intellectual property validity, labor arbitration exclusivity, or matters already conclusively resolved by a final court judgment or arbitration award. Upon receipt of a mediation application, the committee must obtain written consent from all parties; where literacy limitations or physical/cognitive disabilities prevent written consent, an audio-recorded oral consent verified by two committee members shall suffice. Preliminary screening must be completed within three working days of application submission. Acceptance decisions shall be communicated via an official stamped notice, while rejections must include a written explanation citing specific statutory grounds for exclusion (e.g., Articles 5 or 6 of the national regulation) and clearly direct applicants to the competent authority—such as the public security bureau for public order violations or the basic-level people’s court for litigable civil claims. All screening documentation, including application forms, consent records (written or audio), and rejection notices, must be compiled into standardized case files in strict compliance with the Nanjing Municipal Bureau of Justice’s Archival Management Measures for People’s Mediation (2023 edition).

4.2 Conduct of Mediation Sessions

Mediation shall commence within ten working days of case acceptance unless all parties jointly submit a written request for an extension, which may not exceed fifteen additional working days. Sessions may be conducted in person at designated mediation rooms that comply with Nanjing’s municipal accessibility and safety standards, via videoconferencing platforms officially approved by the Jiangsu Provincial Department of Justice (such as ‘SuMediate’), or through shuttle mediation—where parties remain in separate locations and communication is relayed by mediators—when direct contact poses verified safety or emotional risks, including cases involving domestic violence survivors. Mediators must ensure equal speaking time for all participants, refrain from posing leading questions or suggesting specific settlement outcomes, and immediately recuse themselves if they possess familial, financial, or prior professional ties to any party, in accordance with Article 14 of the national People’s Mediation Law. For disputes involving three or more parties or those requiring technical expertise—such as inheritance partitions, land boundary demarcations, or complex co-ownership arrangements—a three-mediator panel shall be convened, with at least one member holding demonstrable subject-matter competence (e.g., a licensed land surveyor, certified family law practitioner, or elder care specialist). Verbatim transcripts of sessions are strictly prohibited; however, a concise session summary must be prepared and signed by all participants within 24 hours. This summary shall include only procedural facts—such as attendance, general topics discussed, and reasons for adjournment—and must bear the explicit notation: “Non-Binding and Inadmissible in Court,” consistent with Article 23 of the national regulation.

4.3 Termination of Mediation and Post-Mediation Pathways

Mediation in Nanjing shall be terminated under any of the following circumstances: (1) the parties execute a written mediation agreement; (2) one or all parties unilaterally or mutually withdraw from mediation, confirmed by signed written notice or verified audio-recorded statement; (3) no consensus is reached after three scheduled mediation sessions and no party requests continuation in writing; or (4) it is discovered during mediation that the dispute involves non-mediable subject matter, such as intellectual property validity, administrative licensing, or other matters excluded by law. Within two working days of termination, the People’s Mediation Committee must issue a “Mediation Closure Notice” using standardized Form NJ-MC-07 issued by the Nanjing Judicial Bureau. This notice shall indicate an outcome code—A for agreement, B for withdrawal, C for impasse, or D for ineligible—and provide clear next-step instructions, such as “Parties may apply for judicial confirmation within 30 days under Article 33 of the national People’s Mediation Law” or “Refer to Gulou District Court for civil litigation.” If both parties jointly request and sign a “Factual Summary Authorization,” the committee may submit to the competent basic-level people’s court a neutral chronology of undisputed facts—including incident dates, witness identities, and property descriptions—but must exclude mediator opinions, settlement offers, or evaluative commentary, in strict compliance with Nanjing Court Guideline No. 12 (2022). All termination-related documents, including closure notices, withdrawal forms, and authorized factual summaries, shall be retained in secure municipal archives for five years, with encrypted digital backups uploaded to the Nanjing Integrated Mediation Platform within 24 hours of issuance.

4.4 Confidentiality and Mediation Records Management

All committee members, staff, and invited experts participating in people’s mediation in Nanjing shall be bound by strict confidentiality obligations under Article 23 of the national People’s Mediation Law. They are prohibited from disclosing any mediation content, party statements, draft agreements, or procedural details to third parties—including family members, employers, or government agencies—except where disclosure is mandated by law (e.g., mandatory reporting of child abuse under the Jiangsu Child Welfare Act) or expressly authorized in writing by all disputing parties. “Mediation records” are defined to include application forms, consent documents, session summaries, closure notices, and court-authorized factual summaries, but exclude personal notes, internal deliberations, or informal communications among mediators. All such records must be stored in locked physical files at the subdistrict or district mediation center and accompanied by encrypted digital copies uploaded to the Nanjing Municipal People’s Mediation Information System within 24 hours of creation. Access to these records is restricted to authorized judicial administrative personnel holding role-based credentials issued by the Municipal Justice Bureau. External access requires a formal written request submitted to the Nanjing Municipal Bureau of Justice citing specific statutory authority—such as a court order under Article 34—with all sensitive identifiers (e.g., ID numbers, medical or financial data) redacted unless parties provide explicit, written waiver. All mediation records shall be securely destroyed after five years through certified physical shredding or digital wiping methods compliant with the Jiangsu Data Security Regulation.

4.5 Drafting and Confirmation of Mediation Agreements

Every mediation agreement concluded under these Rules must contain the following mandatory elements: (1) full names, identification numbers, and contact information of all parties; (2) a clear and concise statement of the factual background of the dispute and the specific mediation requests submitted by the parties; (3) detailed and unambiguous terms of the mediated resolution, including performance obligations, timelines, and methods; (4) original signatures or fingerprints of all parties and the presiding mediator; (5) the exact date of execution; and (6) the official seal of the mediating People’s Mediation Committee. The draft agreement shall be prepared within three working days after consensus is reached and provided to all parties in writing or via secure electronic transmission for review. Parties must confirm their understanding and voluntary acceptance before signing; no signature shall be obtained under duress or without adequate opportunity for review. Should any party submit a written objection to the draft within 24 hours of receipt, the mediation committee shall reconvene within five working days to address the concerns or, if resolution proves unattainable, terminate the process and issue a closure notice. Upon full execution, the agreement becomes legally binding as a civil contract and may be submitted by either party to the competent basic-level people’s court in Nanjing for judicial confirmation within 30 calendar days, in strict accordance with Article 33 of the national People’s Mediation Law.

4.6 Mediator Recusal and Conflict-of-Interest Management

A mediator in Nanjing shall be mandatorily recused if any of the following circumstances exist: (1) being a close relative—defined as spouse, parent, child, sibling, grandparent, or grandchild—of any party or their legal representative; (2) holding a direct personal or financial interest in the outcome of the dispute, including ownership stakes, contractual benefits, or pending claims related to the subject matter; (3) having previously acted as legal counsel, advisor, or representative for any party concerning the same dispute; or (4) any other situation that objectively undermines impartiality, such as prior participation in related administrative decisions, judicial proceedings, or investigative actions involving the parties or the disputed facts. Any party may submit a written recusal request to the chairperson of the People’s Mediation Committee within two working days of becoming aware of the potential conflict, clearly stating factual grounds and supporting evidence. The committee chair—or, if the chair is the subject of the request, the vice-chair or next most senior member—shall issue a written decision on the recusal application within three working days. If recusal is granted, it takes immediate effect, and the challenged mediator is prohibited from participating in any further proceedings related to the case pending the decision. All mediators are required to file an annual conflict-of-interest disclosure form with their district-level justice bureau by January 15 each year and must update this disclosure within 48 hours of any new potential conflict arising during active mediation.

5.1 Formal Requirements and Validity Conditions

Every mediation agreement concluded in Nanjing must be documented in the standardized written form issued by the mediating People’s Mediation Committee, specifically Nanjing Municipal Justice Bureau Form MJ-2024. The agreement shall contain the following mandatory elements: (a) full names and valid identification numbers of all parties; (b) a clear, factual statement identifying the specific civil dispute resolved through mediation; (c) precise terms of the resolution, including performance obligations, deadlines, and methods of fulfillment; (d) original signatures or fingerprints of all parties and at least two mediators who participated in the session; and (e) the official seal of the People’s Mediation Committee that conducted the mediation. Oral agreements are permitted only if all parties jointly submit a written request during the mediation session explicitly waiving a written draft; in such cases, the committee must transcribe the oral agreement verbatim into Form MJ-2024 before closing the session, and all participants must immediately affix their signatures or fingerprints to acknowledge accuracy and voluntary consent. Any agreement procured through coercion, fraud, duress, or material misrepresentation shall be deemed void ab initio. Likewise, agreements whose terms contravene mandatory provisions of Chinese civil law, public order, or good morals are null and unenforceable. Partial agreements resolving only certain issues within a multi-faceted dispute shall remain valid to the extent that the resolved portion is legally and factually separable from unresolved claims. These requirements are anchored in Article 33 of the People’s Mediation Law of the People’s Republic of China and constitute the baseline for judicial confirmation eligibility.

5.2 Judicial Confirmation Procedure and 30-Day Filing Window

Either party to a mediation agreement concluded in Nanjing shall file an application for judicial confirmation with the basic-level people’s court that has jurisdiction over the location of the mediating People’s Mediation Committee within thirty (30) calendar days from the date the agreement is signed or fingerprinted by all parties. The application must include: (i) the original mediation agreement bearing the official seal of the People’s Mediation Committee; (ii) valid identity documents for all parties; (iii) a certification letter issued by the committee verifying that the mediation process fully complied with Articles 17–22 of the national People’s Mediation Law; and (iv) proof of service on the other party if the application is filed unilaterally. Upon receipt, the court shall complete its review within seven working days, examining solely whether the agreement was voluntarily concluded, satisfies statutory formalities, and does not violate public policy or mandatory legal provisions—explicitly refraining from re-litigating factual disputes or reassessing the merits of the settlement. Judicial confirmation, once granted, endows the mediation agreement with the enforceable force of a final civil judgment pursuant to Article 33(2) of the national law. Should the 30-day filing window expire without an application, the agreement retains its validity as a binding civil contract under the Civil Code but forfeits eligibility for direct judicial enforcement, requiring any aggrieved party to initiate separate breach-of-contract litigation to seek remedies.

5.3 Enforceability and Legal Parity with Civil Judgments

A mediation agreement confirmed by a basic-level people’s court in Nanjing pursuant to Article 34 of the People’s Mediation Law of the People’s Republic of China shall possess the same legal force as a final civil judgment and be enforced by the court’s enforcement division through identical compulsory measures. These include, but are not limited to: seizure and public auction of movable or immovable property; garnishment of wages, bank accounts, or other receivables; inclusion of the non-compliant party in the Supreme People’s Court’s Dishonest Debtor List; and imposition of travel bans or high-consumption restrictions under applicable judicial interpretations. Unconfirmed mediation agreements, while retaining binding effect as civil contracts under the Civil Code of the People’s Republic of China, may not serve as the basis for direct enforcement proceedings; instead, aggrieved parties must initiate a separate civil lawsuit seeking specific performance, damages, or declaratory relief. Only the original parties to the agreement or third parties who can demonstrate a direct, legitimate interest materially and adversely affected by its terms shall have standing to challenge a confirmed agreement. Such challenges must be filed with the confirming court either prior to the commencement of enforcement or during the enforcement process, and shall be adjudicated in accordance with Nanjing Intermediate People’s Court Guideline No. NJFY-ENF-2023 on enforcement protocols for confirmed mediation agreements.

5.4 Invalidity and Revocation of Mediation Agreements

A mediation agreement concluded in Nanjing shall be deemed null and void if any of the following conditions exist: (a) its terms violate mandatory provisions of Chinese law or contravene public order and good customs; (b) it purports to resolve matters expressly excluded from mediation under Article 4 of the national People’s Mediation Law, such as criminal liability, administrative penalties, or disputes subject to exclusive jurisdiction by other state organs; (c) it is executed by a person lacking legal capacity without the prior written consent of their statutory representative; or (d) the parties collude with intent to harm the interests of the state, collective entities, or third parties. Additionally, an agreement may be revoked if procured under (i) material fraud or deliberate concealment that substantially affected a party’s consent; (ii) duress, coercion, or undue influence exerted by a mediator or any third party; or (iii) a significant misunderstanding regarding the essential nature or legal consequences of the agreement. Any petition seeking invalidation or revocation must be filed with the competent basic-level people’s court within one year from the date the petitioner knew or should have known of the defect, accompanied by credible evidence substantiating the claim. Legally, void agreements are treated as never having existed; revoked agreements lose effect retroactively, and parties must restore any benefits received, except where restitution would violate public interest or is objectively impossible.

6.1 Administrative Finality and Inter-Agency Coordination

The Nanjing Municipal Justice Bureau and the Nanjing Intermediate People’s Court are hereby designated as the sole joint authorities empowered to interpret these Implementation Rules, in accordance with Article 34 of the People’s Mediation Law of the People’s Republic of China. To ensure consistent application and operational coherence, district-level judicial administrative departments and basic-level people’s courts shall convene mandatory coordination meetings every calendar quarter—specifically during the first week of January, April, July, and October. These meetings shall serve three core functions: (1) harmonizing local mediation guidance standards with municipal and national legal frameworks; (2) exchanging anonymized datasets on mediation outcomes, including settlement rates, dispute categories, recurrence indicators, and demographic trends; and (3) jointly resolving discrepancies in the interpretation or implementation of procedural or substantive provisions arising in practice. All mediation agreements lawfully concluded prior to the effective date of these Rules shall retain full legal validity under the regulatory framework in force at the time of their conclusion and remain eligible for judicial confirmation under then-applicable procedures. Any People’s Mediation Committee newly established on or after the effective date must achieve full compliance—with respect to committee composition (3–9 members, inclusive of at least one female member and, where ethnic minorities constitute ≥5% of the local population, at least one minority representative), mediator qualifications, and procedural safeguards—within 90 calendar days of its establishment. The Nanjing Municipal Justice Bureau is further designated as the official custodian and publisher of all standardized mediation documentation, including but not limited to: (a) model mediation application forms; (b) written consent templates affirming voluntary participation; (c) mediation record templates compliant with confidentiality safeguards under Article 23 of the national law; and (d) procedural advisories tailored to urban districts (such as Gulou, Jianye, and Qinhuai) and rural counties (including Lishui, Gaochun, and Pukou), thereby ensuring uniform, high-quality implementation of people’s mediation citywide.

6.2 Municipal Support Obligations and Mediator Risk Protection

The Nanjing municipal government and its subordinate district governments shall bear a legally binding obligation to provide annual fiscal subsidies for grassroots mediators, with subsidy tiers calibrated according to jurisdiction type and verified workload. Urban People’s Mediation Committees—including those in Gulou, Xuanwu, Jianye, Qinhuai, and other core districts—shall receive RMB 3,000 to 5,000 per mediator annually, contingent upon each mediator handling no fewer than 50 mediated cases per year. Rural committees—in Lishui, Gaochun, Pukou, Luhe, and similar areas—shall receive RMB 2,000 to 3,500 per mediator annually, provided they mediate at least 30 cases per year. All caseload certifications and subsidy adjustments must be verified and approved by the Nanjing Municipal Justice Bureau by February 28 each year. Any injury, disability, or death sustained by a registered mediator while performing official duties—including on-site mediation at residences, public spaces, or during community outreach activities—shall qualify for compensation equivalent to statutory work-related injury benefits under the State Council’s Work-Related Injury Insurance Regulations (Order No. 586). This compensation shall be administered through the Nanjing Mediator Occupational Risk Protection Fund, jointly managed by the Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau and the Municipal Justice Bureau, with all eligible claims processed and disbursed within 30 working days of submission. In the event of a mediator’s death in the line of duty, surviving dependents shall receive a lump-sum bereavement allowance of RMB 200,000 and annual educational subsidies of RMB 10,000 per dependent child until age 18, or until age 22 if the child is enrolled in full-time higher education. The Municipal Justice Bureau is further authorized to implement an annual “Outstanding Mediator” recognition program and disburse continuing education grants of up to RMB 2,000 per mediator for accredited training in conflict resolution, civil law updates, or psychological first aid, subject to performance evaluation and budgetary approval.

6.3 Effective Date and Transitional Arrangements

These Implementation Rules shall enter into force on January 1, 2025. All mediation proceedings initiated prior to this date shall be completed in accordance with the procedural rules and committee structures in effect at the time of initiation, and any resulting mediation agreements shall retain full legal enforceability under Article 33 of the People’s Mediation Law of the People’s Republic of China. Any mediation process commenced on or after January 1, 2025, must strictly comply with the requirements set forth in Chapters 2 through 5 of these Rules, including but not limited to committee composition, mediator qualifications, procedural safeguards, and documentation standards. People’s Mediation Committees lawfully established and operating as of December 31, 2024, are granted a 90-day grace period—extending until March 31, 2025—to adjust their membership to satisfy the gender and ethnic inclusion mandates specified in Section 2.2 and to revise internal operating procedures to align with the updated mediation workflow. Such revisions must include implementing mandatory protocols for recording voluntary consent and providing parties with clear written advisories regarding the 30-day window for judicial confirmation of mediation agreements.

1.1 Legislative Purpose and Legal Basis

In accordance with Article 1 of the People’s Mediation Law of the People’s Republic of China—which stipulates that the law is enacted pursuant to the Constitution to improve the people’s mediation system, regulate mediation activities, promptly resolve civil disputes, and maintain social harmony and stability—and in full alignment with Articles 1–35 of the same law as well as the Jiangsu Provincial Regulations on People’s Mediation (effective version: 2021), the Nanjing Municipal People’s Government hereby issues these Implementation Rules pursuant to its authority under Article 32 of the national law and delegated powers under provincial legislation. These Rules aim to achieve four concrete objectives: (1) standardize the establishment, composition, and operational procedures of all People’s Mediation Committees within Nanjing’s administrative jurisdiction; (2) ensure that mediators meet minimum qualification thresholds and strictly adhere to ethical and disciplinary standards; (3) guarantee that mediation agreements are eligible for judicial confirmation by basic-level people’s courts within 30 days as mandated by Article 33 of the national law, thereby securing their legal enforceability; and (4) institutionalize sustained municipal fiscal support for mediators, including compensation for injury, disability, or death incurred while performing official duties. These Rules shall have binding effect on all district-level justice bureaus, township governments, subdistrict offices, and People’s Mediation Committees throughout Nanjing City.

1.2 Scope of Application and Territorial Jurisdiction

These Rules apply to all civil disputes mediated by any People’s Mediation Committee registered with a district-level judicial administrative department in Nanjing City, including but not limited to committees in Xuanwu, Qinhuai, Jianye, Gulou, Yuhuatai, Qixia, Pukou, Luhe, Lishui, and Gaochun districts. Covered disputes must concern civil rights and obligations among natural persons, legal entities, or unincorporated organizations, specifically involving property relations, neighbor conflicts, family matters, minor torts, or other civil disputes explicitly enumerated in Article 2 of the national People’s Mediation Law. The Rules expressly exclude disputes involving criminal acts, public security penalties, administrative adjudication, matters subject to mandatory labor arbitration, or cases where a party lacks legal capacity and is not properly represented by a statutory agent. Every mediation case must be formally recorded in the Nanjing Judicial Administration Mediation Case Registry within three working days of acceptance. Territorial jurisdiction shall be determined by the defendant’s domicile or the location where the dispute arose, in strict accordance with joint guidance issued by the Nanjing Intermediate People’s Court and the Municipal Justice Bureau.

1.3 Foundational Principles and Oversight Framework

All people’s mediation activities in Nanjing City shall strictly adhere to five foundational principles derived from Articles 3, 4, and 17 of the national People’s Mediation Law: (1) Voluntariness—parties must provide written consent prior to the commencement of mediation and retain the unconditional right to withdraw at any stage without penalty; (2) Equality—all parties shall enjoy equal procedural rights irrespective of gender, ethnicity, occupation, education level, or socioeconomic status; (3) No-fee requirement—mediation services, including document preparation and agreement certification, shall be provided entirely free of charge, with operational costs covered by district-level fiscal allocations; (4) Impartiality and confidentiality—mediators must proactively disclose any actual or potential conflicts of interest and are prohibited from disclosing case details except as mandated by law or with the written consent of all parties; and (5) Legality—mediated agreements must not contravene mandatory legal provisions, public order, or good morals. A dual oversight framework is hereby established: district judicial bureaus are responsible for supervising committee formation, mediator training, and performance evaluation, while basic-level people’s courts—including Gulou District Court and Jiangning District Court—shall review mediation procedures upon request and process judicial confirmation applications within 30 days of agreement execution. Under no circumstances may any government official, committee member, or third party coerce parties into mediation or impose settlement terms.

2.1 Establishment Criteria and Territorial Anchoring

Pursuant to Article 8 of the People’s Mediation Law of the People’s Republic of China, a People’s Mediation Committee shall be established in every residents’ committee, villagers’ committee, subdistrict office, and township government within Nanjing City. Establishment is mandatory under any of the following triggers: (1) an urban community with 3,000 or more registered residents; (2) an administrative village with 1,500 or more registered residents; or (3) any locality that reports ten or more civil disputes per quarter to its corresponding judicial administrative office. Each legally constituted grassroots autonomous organization, as officially recognized by the Nanjing Civil Affairs Bureau, shall host exactly one primary People’s Mediation Committee; the creation of multiple committees within a single jurisdictional unit is strictly prohibited, as is the omission of a committee in any qualifying unit. The operational territory of each committee must align precisely with the official geographic boundaries documented in the latest civil affairs registry, specifically referencing the boundary maps filed under Nanjing Municipal Administrative Division Code NJ-ADM-2023. To ensure service integrity and prevent territorial overlap or coverage gaps, district-level Justice Bureaus are required to conduct quarterly verifications of all committee jurisdictions and submit compliance reports to the Nanjing Municipal Justice Bureau by the 10th day of January, April, July, and October each year.

2.2 Composition Requirements, Term Limits, and Representative Inclusion

Each People’s Mediation Committee in Nanjing City shall consist of no fewer than three and no more than nine members, including exactly one chairperson and up to two vice-chairpersons, whose appointments shall reflect the complexity and volume of local caseloads as assessed by the district-level Justice Bureau. To ensure inclusive representation, at least one-third of all committee members must be women. Furthermore, in any township or subdistrict where ethnic minorities constitute 5% or more of the resident population—according to the latest official data from the Nanjing Ethnic Affairs Commission—at least one committee member must belong to a state-recognized minority group. All members shall serve fixed terms of three years, commencing uniformly on January 1 of the appointment year. Reappointment for a second consecutive term is permitted only once, unless the district-level Justice Bureau issues a written exception based on documented exceptional performance or a verified local shortage of qualified mediators. Members representing gender or ethnic minority interests are required to participate directly in case triage meetings and must co-sign any mediation agreement that substantively affects the rights or interests of the groups they represent, thereby ensuring procedural equity and substantive inclusion in dispute resolution outcomes.

2.3 Appointment Procedures and Institutional Accountability

The appointment of People’s Mediation Committee members in Nanjing shall follow a standardized four-step process. First, candidates must be nominated either through an open vote at a residents’ meeting or villagers’ assembly, or via formal recommendation by the community Party branch. Second, the subdistrict or township judicial administrative office shall conduct a thorough background check and verify that each candidate meets the eligibility criteria stipulated in Article 14 of the national People’s Mediation Law, including integrity, legal literacy, and absence of disqualifying conditions. Third, the names, qualifications, and signed conflict-of-interest declarations of all shortlisted candidates shall be publicly displayed for seven consecutive days both on the community bulletin board and on the official Nanjing Justice Portal to ensure transparency and public oversight. Fourth, upon successful completion of the公示 period without substantiated objections, the district-level Justice Bureau shall issue a formal appointment decision within 15 working days and electronically file the appointee’s information into the Jiangsu Mediator Registry System. In addition to this appointment protocol, each People’s Mediation Committee is subject to dual accountability: it must submit detailed quarterly activity reports to its local residents’ or villagers’ assembly and undergo an annual compliance audit conducted by the district Justice Bureau. Furthermore, by March 31 of each year, all committees are required to publish key performance data—including total mediation cases, resolution rates, and substantiated complaint records—on the Nanjing Government Open Data Platform to enhance public trust and institutional transparency.

2.4 Functions and Operational Responsibilities of Committees

People’s Mediation Committees in Nanjing shall perform the following statutory duties as derived from Articles 17–22 of the national People’s Mediation Law: (1) mediate civil disputes falling within their territorial jurisdiction that involve neighborhood relations, family matters, small claims not exceeding RMB 50,000, and minor property conflicts; (2) conduct monthly dispute risk screening using the standardized “Community Dispute Risk Assessment Form” issued by the Nanjing Municipal Justice Bureau, with results submitted to the subdistrict or township judicial office by the fifth working day of each month; (3) maintain a publicly accessible mediation logbook—available for inspection during regular office hours—that records, for each case, the date of acceptance, identities of parties (with privacy safeguards), issue category, mediation outcome, and status of agreement execution; (4) immediately refer to competent authorities any matter involving criminal conduct, domestic violence, or civil claims exceeding RMB 50,000, with such referrals completed within 24 hours of identification and documented in the case file; (5) organize biannual public legal education sessions—once in spring and once in autumn—focused on citizens’ mediation rights, procedural safeguards, and conflict prevention, in coordination with local community centers and schools; and (6) actively coordinate with nearby police stations and basic-level people’s courts to implement joint mediation under Nanjing’s “Three-in-One” integrated dispute resolution mechanism, particularly for complex or high-tension cases involving multi-party interests or public safety concerns, as endorsed by the Nanjing Intermediate People’s Court.

3.1 Eligibility Criteria and Disqualification Conditions

Mediators serving in Nanjing City must be Chinese citizens aged 23 or older, reflecting local standards for civic maturity and judgment. They must possess at least a high school diploma or an equivalent vocational qualification and have continuously resided in the community they serve for no less than one year prior to appointment. Candidates shall provide documented proof of good moral character through a formal recommendation issued by their local residents’ committee or current employer. Additionally, all prospective mediators must demonstrate basic legal literacy by successfully completing the foundational mediation training course administered by the Nanjing Municipal Justice Bureau, which covers core principles of civil law, mediation ethics, and procedural norms. Individuals are categorically disqualified if they have any criminal record—including convictions for public order offenses—or are currently under investigation by disciplinary or supervisory authorities. Concurrent service as legal counsel, business representative, or financial stakeholder for any party involved in disputes within the mediator’s jurisdiction also constitutes grounds for disqualification. Furthermore, persons who were previously removed from a People’s Mediation Committee within the past five years shall not be reappointed. Appointment is expressly prohibited for individuals with active civil incapacity, those diagnosed with severe mental illness by a hospital rated Grade II-A or higher, or anyone with unresolved conflicts of interest involving immediate family members of disputing parties. These criteria align strictly with Articles 14–16 of the national People’s Mediation Law while integrating Nanjing’s enhanced urban governance standards.

3.2 Professional Duties and Ethical Obligations

Mediators in Nanjing City shall conduct all mediation sessions strictly in accordance with the principles of voluntariness, equality, and legality as stipulated in Article 3 of the People’s Mediation Law of the People’s Republic of China. Prior to initiating any mediation, mediators must proactively disclose any actual or potential conflict of interest and immediately recuse themselves if such a conflict exists or is reasonably perceived to impair impartiality. Recording of mediation sessions—whether audio, video, or written—is strictly prohibited without the prior written consent of all parties. Mediators may not share case details with third parties except to the extent necessary for judicial confirmation under Article 33, and ex parte communications with any party during the mediation process are expressly forbidden. Mediators are obligated to clearly explain to all parties the legal effect of a mediation agreement, including the critical 30-day window for applying for judicial confirmation, and must ensure that each party signs an informed consent form acknowledging their understanding of procedural rights and voluntary participation. Furthermore, every mediator must complete at least 16 hours of annual continuing education administered by the Nanjing Municipal Bureau of Justice, covering updates to civil law, emerging local dispute patterns (such as neighborhood property conflicts, migrant labor issues, and elderly care disputes), and trauma-informed communication techniques. Any violation of these professional duties and ethical obligations shall constitute grounds for disciplinary action pursuant to Section 3.3 of these Rules.

3.3 Disciplinary Procedures and Accountability Mechanisms

A three-stage disciplinary process is established to address alleged misconduct by mediators in Nanjing City. First, any party to a mediation, committee member, or judicial administrative office may file a written complaint with supporting evidence to the subdistrict or township judicial office within 90 days of the alleged violation. Second, the judicial office must complete a preliminary review within 15 working days; if the complaint is substantiated, it shall forward the case to the district-level Bureau of Justice with a formal recommendation for action. Third, the district Bureau, in joint consultation with the relevant People’s Mediation Committee, shall convene a hearing within 30 days, during which the accused mediator has the right to present a defense and submit evidence. Tiered sanctions shall be imposed based on the severity of the breach: a formal written warning for minor infractions such as procedural delays; suspension from mediation duties for up to six months for violations of confidentiality; and permanent removal from the mediator roster for serious offenses including bribery, falsification of mediation agreements, or repeated demonstrations of bias. All final disciplinary decisions shall be recorded in the Nanjing Mediator Integrity Registry, which is accessible to municipal oversight bodies but shielded from public disclosure unless the sanction involves permanent removal. These procedures comply with Article 35 of the national People’s Mediation Law and fully preserve the mediator’s statutory right to seek administrative reconsideration.

3.4 Appointment, Term of Office, and Renewal Procedures for Mediators

Mediators in Nanjing City shall be nominated by their local residents’ committee, workplace union, or a recognized professional association and formally appointed by the township or subdistrict People’s Mediation Committee only after thorough verification of eligibility under Section 3.1 of these Rules. Each appointment carries a fixed term of three years, uniformly commencing on January 1 of the appointment year. Reappointment for a second consecutive term is permitted, but no mediator may serve more than two consecutive terms unless exceptional circumstances are documented and approved by the district Justice Bureau. Reappointment eligibility requires that the mediator has completed all mandatory annual training, maintained a case resolution rate of at least 70% during the prior term, and received no disciplinary sanctions. Upon term expiration or early departure for any reason, the mediator must comply with a formal handover protocol: transfer all non-confidential case logs to the committee secretary, return official seals, mediation materials, and identification credentials within five working days, and participate in an exit interview conducted by the district judicial office to document lessons learned and procedural feedback. All initial appointments and renewals must be registered in the Nanjing Municipal Mediator Roster within 10 working days of the appointment decision and reported quarterly to the Jiangsu Provincial Department of Justice for consolidated oversight and statistical analysis.

4.1 Case Acceptance and Preliminary Screening

Nanjing People’s Mediation Committees shall accept only civil disputes falling within the scope of Article 2 of the People’s Mediation Law—specifically, those concerning civil rights and obligations arising from property relations, neighborhood conflicts, family matters, or minor torts—and shall categorically exclude cases involving criminal conduct, administrative penalties, intellectual property validity, labor arbitration exclusivity, or matters already conclusively resolved by a final court judgment or arbitration award. Upon receipt of a mediation application, the committee must obtain written consent from all parties; where literacy limitations or physical/cognitive disabilities prevent written consent, an audio-recorded oral consent verified by two committee members shall suffice. Preliminary screening must be completed within three working days of application submission. Acceptance decisions shall be communicated via an official stamped notice, while rejections must include a written explanation citing specific statutory grounds for exclusion (e.g., Articles 5 or 6 of the national regulation) and clearly direct applicants to the competent authority—such as the public security bureau for public order violations or the basic-level people’s court for litigable civil claims. All screening documentation, including application forms, consent records (written or audio), and rejection notices, must be compiled into standardized case files in strict compliance with the Nanjing Municipal Bureau of Justice’s Archival Management Measures for People’s Mediation (2023 edition).

Mediation shall commence within ten working days of case acceptance unless all parties jointly submit a written request for an extension, which may not exceed fifteen additional working days. Sessions may be conducted in person at designated mediation rooms that comply with Nanjing’s municipal accessibility and safety standards, via videoconferencing platforms officially approved by the Jiangsu Provincial Department of Justice (such as ‘SuMediate’), or through shuttle mediation—where parties remain in separate locations and communication is relayed by mediators—when direct contact poses verified safety or emotional risks, including cases involving domestic violence survivors. For disputes involving three or more parties or those requiring technical expertise—such as inheritance partitions, land boundary demarcations, or complex co-ownership arrangements—a three-mediator panel shall be convened, with at least one member holding demonstrable subject-matter competence (e.g., a licensed land surveyor, certified family law practitioner, or elder care specialist). Verbatim transcripts of sessions are strictly prohibited; however, a concise session summary must be prepared and signed by all participants within 24 hours. This summary shall include only procedural facts—such as attendance, general topics discussed, and reasons for adjournment—and must bear the explicit notation: “Non-Binding and Inadmissible in Court,” consistent with Article 23 of the national regulation.

Within two working days of termination, the People’s Mediation Committee must issue a “Mediation Closure Notice” using standardized Form NJ-MC-07 issued by the Nanjing Judicial Bureau. This notice shall indicate an outcome code—A for agreement, B for withdrawal, C for impasse, or D for ineligible—and provide clear next-step instructions, such as “Parties may apply for judicial confirmation within 30 days under Article 33 of the national People’s Mediation Law” or “Refer to Gulou District Court for civil litigation.” If both parties jointly request and sign a “Factual Summary Authorization,” the committee may submit to the competent basic-level people’s court a neutral chronology of undisputed facts—including incident dates, witness identities, and property descriptions—but must exclude mediator opinions, settlement offers, or evaluative commentary, in strict compliance with Nanjing Court Guideline No. 12 (2022). All termination-related documents, including closure notices, withdrawal forms, and authorized factual summaries, shall be retained in secure municipal archives for five years, with encrypted digital backups uploaded to the Nanjing Integrated Mediation Platform within 24 hours of issuance.

They are prohibited from disclosing any mediation content, party statements, draft agreements, or procedural details to third parties—including family members, employers, or government agencies—except where disclosure is mandated by law (e.g., mandatory reporting of child abuse under the Jiangsu Child Welfare Act) or expressly authorized in writing by all disputing parties. “Mediation records” are defined to include application forms, consent documents, session summaries, closure notices, and court-authorized factual summaries, but exclude personal notes, internal deliberations, or informal communications among mediators.
